tldr: This paper presents a blind grasp reflex policy trained with reinforcement learning. Without cameras or tactile sensors, it uses only joint encoder feedback to stably grasp unseen objects. The result acts as a reusable, modular hand controller that pairs seamlessly with independent arm controllers.
hero_caption: Overview of the proposed system architecture. The arm module handles global reaching, while the hand module performs local contact control using proprioception (joint encoders) alone. A simple bidirectional interface—an engage signal to start grasping and a learned grasp score to signal completion—lets you swap out arm controllers without retraining the hand.
overview:
Think about how humans pick up an object. We look at it to reach our hand toward its rough location. But during the final moments of finger contact, we do not need to keep staring. We can reliably grasp it using touch alone, even with our eyes closed. In contrast, conventional robotic hand research often relies heavily on global visual observations—such as camera images, point clouds, or 3D object poses—to control all arm and finger joints jointly. When a system depends too much on vision, it easily breaks under small changes in object appearance, messy backgrounds, or arm positioning errors.

To address this, the authors return to a simple principle: "See to reach, feel to grasp." The arm is responsible only for bringing the hand close to the target. Meanwhile, a 20-DoF anthropomorphic robotic hand learns a "blind grasp reflex" through reinforcement learning. Without external cameras, object meshes, or specialized tactile sensors, it detects contact and wraps around objects using only joint encoder history. In addition, the hand predicts a "grasp score" that indicates whether the object is securely held. This provides a bidirectional interface that tells the arm exactly when it is safe to transition to post-grasp tasks like lifting or carrying.

Trained in simulation using privileged teacher-student distillation, this policy achieves grasping without any vision at the wrist or fingers. It posts remarkable success rates: 96% on the YCB dataset and 95% across more than 3,000 objects in GraspXL. On physical hardware, the same frozen policy readily grasps 29 diverse household items. It also pairs out of the box with unseen arm behaviors, including VLM-guided tabletop tidying and lightbulb screwing.
contributions: Developed a local hand policy that stably grasps unseen objects using only joint encoder history (proprioception), without cameras or tactile sensors.
Designed a scalar grasp score learned self-supervised from task rewards, creating a clean, flexible interface that tells the arm when a grasp is secure.

Discovered that despite receiving zero contact geometry inputs, the learned grasp score strongly aligns with a classical physics-based measure of grasp stability (Ferrari-Canny epsilon metric, mean correlation of 0.77).

Demonstrated modularity by pairing the frozen hand policy with diverse tasks—such as lightbulb screwing and VLM-guided manipulation—as well as novel robot arms and mounting configurations without retraining.

sections.heading: Seeing to Reach, Feeling to Grasp: Why Make the Hand Blind?
sections.summary: Dexterous grasping with multi-fingered hands is fundamentally a contact-rich feedback control problem. However, vision-dependent pipelines often fail under reaching errors or visual shifts. This section explains the motivation behind decoupling arm reaching from hand contact control to build a blind grasp reflex driven purely by joint encoder history.
sections.details:
Parallel-jaw grippers can secure many objects simply by squeezing them between two frictional pads. Anthropomorphic hands, by contrast, rely on where multiple local contact points form and how contact forces balance. Modeling these interactions accurately is very difficult without dense tactile skins across the entire hand.

Most prior learning-based methods feed point clouds, images, or 3D object poses directly into a single policy controlling both the arm and the fingers. Tying finger contact control to global visual features leaves the system vulnerable to distribution shifts in object geometry, initial poses, and background clutter, hurting generalization.

Humans, on the other hand, do not stare at their fingertips once their hand is in place; proprioceptive and tactile feedback guide the fingers. This work adopts that separation of concerns: the arm handles global reaching, while the hand handles local contact adaptation. The hand policy receives no camera frames, object meshes, or even arm joint states. It looks only at its own joint encoder history to reflexively wrap around and stabilize objects.

Another critical question is deciding when an object is securely held. Contact proceeds at different speeds depending on object stiffness and geometry. Relying on fixed-duration timers leads to premature drops or wasted pauses. In this work, the hand outputs a continuous grasp score that measures grasp security. This forms a bidirectional interface that tells the arm precisely when to begin downstream manipulation.

captions.F1: The proposed approach grasping diverse real-world objects without visual inputs or geometric priors. From soft plush toys to bowls, tape rolls, hand tools, and lightbulbs, the identical hand policy secures them all.

sections.heading: Related Work: Moving Beyond Costly Tactile Skins and Point Clouds
sections.summary: This section reviews vision-based dexterous grasping and tactile sensing approaches, highlighting what makes this work unique. Unlike methods needing expensive tactile arrays or global point cloud inputs, this approach infers contacts implicitly using standard joint encoders.
sections.details:
### II-A Vision-Based Dexterous Grasping
Prior systems such as DexPoint, UniDexGrasp, and DextrAH train arm and hand behaviors jointly using point clouds or RGB-D frames. Some incorporate hand-centric distance representations to improve robustness, but fingertip contact still relies heavily on external vision. As a result, they remain vulnerable to visual occlusions and arm tracking lag. It is also difficult to transplant their trained hand controllers onto different reach planners or novel robot arms. Decoupling the hand from the arm solves this reusability problem directly.

### II-B Blind and Proprioceptive Grasping
Approaches that grasp without vision often depend on underactuated hands with compliant joints, or on high-resolution tactile sensors on fingertips. Recent efforts combine tactile simulation with reinforcement learning, but closing the sim-to-real gap for tactile data remains challenging.

In contrast, this paper shows that a standard rigid-surface robot hand can infer contact dynamics using only its joint encoder history (proprioception). Furthermore, while prior grasp stability estimators rely on explicit ground-truth labels like lift outcomes, this policy learns a scalar transition signal in a self-supervised way as part of its own action space.

sections.heading: Feeling Contacts: The Architecture and Grasp Score Learning
sections.summary: The system features three modular tiers: an arm module, a hand module, and a low-level velocity controller. An RL teacher trained with privileged sim data is distilled into a blind student using only joint histories, while simultaneously learning a scalar grasp score driven by task rewards.
sections.details:
### Architecture Overview
The framework consists of three tiers, as illustrated in Fig. F2. The arm module outputs a target wrist pose and an engage signal $g_t$. The hand module outputs target joint angles and a grasp score $\gamma_t \in [0, 1]$. A low-level controller running at 1 kHz converts these targets into smooth velocity commands, sending PD torque commands with gravity compensation to every joint.

### III-A Hand Policy Design and Distillation
The hand action space includes 20 joint angle targets and the scalar grasp score $\gamma_t$. To stabilize exploration and encourage natural grasp postures, the action is regularized with a prior derived from Principal Component Analysis (PCA) on human grasp data:
$q^{\mathrm{tgt}}_t = \beta (W^\top W(\tilde{q}_t - \bar{q}) + \bar{q}) + (1 - \beta)\tilde{q}_t$
where $\beta$ controls the strength of the prior.

- ### III-A 1 Privileged Teacher Training
In MuJoCo Warp, a teacher policy is trained with PPO. It observes contact flags across all hand links $c^{\mathrm{full}}_t$, the object position relative to the palm $d^{\mathrm{palm}}_t$, and current joint angles $q_t$. The critic also accesses the object's absolute pose and linear/angular velocity.

- ### III-A 2 Distillation to a Blind Student (DAgger)
The student policy, deployed on the real robot, receives only the past $H=5$ steps (about 0.4 seconds) of joint angles $q$ and joint tracking errors $\Delta q = q - q^{\mathrm{cmd}}$. When a finger hits an obstacle and stops moving, a sustained tracking error emerges between commanded and measured angles. Through DAgger distillation, the student learns to infer contact locations implicitly from these error patterns without any external sensors.

### III-B Implicitly Learned Grasp Score
The grasp score $\gamma_t$ serves as a transition trigger in a finite-state machine (FSM) that shifts the arm from reaching to lifting during training. Lifting before a solid grasp causes drops and loses task rewards, while waiting too long delays rewards. Driven purely by this task feedback, the policy naturally learns to output an accurate measure of grasp stability without explicit labels.

### III-C Arm-Hand Coordination
The arm triggers hand grasping by setting $g_t = 1$ once it enters a target zone near the object. When the grasp score crosses a threshold, the arm proceeds to post-grasp actions like lifting or screwing. If the object slips and the score drops mid-motion, the system can autonomously revert to the reach phase to re-grasp.

sections.heading: Experimental Results: >95% Grasp Success and Physics-Based Alignment
sections.summary: Evaluations in simulation and on real hardware demonstrate high grasp success, robustness against dynamic target shifts, and broad workspace coverage. Crucially, the learned grasp score closely mirrors the classical Ferrari-Canny epsilon metric for force closure.
sections.details:
### IV-A Experimental Setup
The physical platform features a 7-DoF Flexiv Rizon 4 arm and a 20-DoF Robotis HX5-D20-MRT 5-finger hand. The hand policy runs at 11.9 Hz, the arm module at 200 Hz, and the low-level controller at 1 kHz as asynchronous processes. Simulation training runs in MuJoCo Warp across 4,096 parallel environments on a single Nvidia L40S GPU, finishing in roughly 4 GPU hours.

### IV-B & C Grasping Performance
The method was compared against a scripted baseline, an end-to-end (E2E) RL baseline using point clouds (adapted from RobustDexGrasp), and an ablation using a fixed timer instead of the grasp score.
- On static grasp success, the E2E baseline performs well, but the proposed method matches it, scoring 96% on YCB objects and 95% across 3,028 GraspXL objects.
- In dynamic grasping tests where the object moves mid-grasp, the E2E baseline degrades significantly outside its training distribution. In contrast, the modular system keeps a very high success rate because the arm updates wrist targets online while the hand reflex handles local contact (see Fig. F3).
- On physical hardware, the policy successfully grasped all 29 household objects tested, spanning wide variations in geometry, size, and material (Fig. F5).

### IV-D Physical Validity of the Grasp Score
To verify what the learned score $\gamma_t$ captures, it was compared to the Ferrari-Canny $\epsilon$-metric, a classical measure of grasp stability based on friction cones. Remarkably, without ever observing contact geometry, the student policy's grasp score showed a strong Spearman rank correlation with this physics metric (overall episode mean $\bar{\rho} = +0.77$, with $+0.78$ on successes and $+0.61$ on failures).

### IV-E & F Cross-Embodiment, Novel Tasks, and Ablations
The frozen hand policy paired zero-shot with tabletop tidying guided by a VLM (RexOmni), a lightbulb-screwing rotation task (Fig. F4), and real-time obstacle avoidance using a QP controller (Fig. F8). It also transferred seamlessly to different arms (Franka Panda, UR5e, Kinova Gen3) and unusual base orientations, including ceiling and wall mounts (Fig. F7).
Ablation studies showed that a human grasp prior weight of $\beta = 0.5$ balances dexterity with posture quality, and feeding joint tracking errors $\Delta q = q - q^{\mathrm{cmd}}$ is critical for sensing motor resistance.

sections.heading: Takeaway: Reframing Dexterous Hands as Reusable Grasp Skills
sections.summary: This study shows that a proprioceptive blind grasp reflex paired with a grasp score decouples hand control from specific arms and visual pipelines, turning dexterous grasping into a modular, reusable building block.
sections.details:
This paper presented a dexterous hand policy that wraps around and stabilizes diverse objects using proprioceptive feedback alone. Its core strength lies in condensing arm-hand coordination into an ultra-lean bidirectional interface: an engage signal to start, and a grasp score to report stability.

Comprehensive simulation evaluations, physical tests on 29 diverse objects, cross-embodiment transfers, and tasks like bulb screwing and VLM integration show that this contact adaptation generalizes broadly. Instead of training monolithic end-to-end policies for every new robot and task, dexterous grasping can be treated as a modular hand skill that plugs into any arm controller.

takeaways: Relying on hand proprioception (joint tracking error histories) instead of global visual inputs for finger contact control yields far greater robustness to distribution shifts and reaching errors.
Without explicit stability labels, the scalar grasp score naturally aligns with physical grasp metrics (Ferrari-Canny epsilon) purely through task rewards tied to lift success.
Decoupling arm reach from hand contact via a minimal interface makes the grasp policy reusable, enabling zero-shot transfer across diverse arm controllers and new robot embodiments.
limitations: The approach has not been thoroughly evaluated on very thin or small objects (like cards or coins) that demand sliding fingertips underneath surfaces, or on precision pinch grasps.
Real-world evaluations on the 29 household objects remain qualitative demonstrations, lacking repeated-trial statistical success rates for each object.
The system assumes the arm can bring the hand close to the target object; recovery strategies for severe reaching failures depend on the upstream arm controller.
